dok_rationale: Part (c) coordinates binomial parameters, a standardized distance, approximation conditions, and competing meanings of rare and impossible to assess a coach's claim and its consequence.
stem: Suppose the same 70 percent free-throw shooter takes 100 attempts under comparable conditions and makes 58. Let $X$ be the number of makes if the career-rate model still applies.\par\smallskip \textbf{Coach:} ``Anything under 60 makes is impossible for a 70 percent shooter, so 58 proves the career rate no longer applies.''\par \textbf{Analyst:} ``A result can be unusual without being impossible; compare 58 with the model's mean and standard deviation.''
first_take: Whose statement is more defensible, the coach's or the analyst's? Name one quantity you would check.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: State $n$ and $p$ for $X$ and write the formulas for the binomial mean and standard deviation.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Without calculating yet, interpret the model's mean and standard deviation in the context of many sets of 100 free throws.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Compute $\mu_X$, $\sigma_X$, and the $z$-score of 58. Check $np$ and $n(1-p)$ to decide whether a normal approximation is reasonable. Is 58 unusual? Adjudicate the two statements, distinguish ``unusual'' from ``impossible,'' and explain what the coach's claim could mislead a reader into believing.

answers.a: Here $n=100$ and $p=0.70$. For a binomial count, $\mu_X=np$ and $\sigma_X=\sqrt{np(1-p)}$.
answers.b: Across many comparable sets of 100 shots under the 0.70 model, the number made would average $\mu_X$ makes. A set's number made would typically differ from that mean by about $\sigma_X$ makes; neither parameter guarantees the result in one set.
answers.c: $\mu_X=100(0.70)=70$ makes and $\sigma_X=\sqrt{100(0.70)(0.30)}=\sqrt{21}=4.5826\approx4.6$ makes. Thus $z=(58-70)/4.5826=-2.6186\approx-2.6$. Also, $np=70$ and $n(1-p)=30$, both at least 10, so a normal approximation is reasonable. Because 58 is about 2.6 standard deviations below the mean, it is unusual. The analyst is warranted: unusual means low probability under the model, not zero probability. In fact, the exact binomial probability $P(X\leq58)\approx0.00717$, and $P(X<60)\approx0.01250$, so fewer than 60 remains possible. The coach turns an expected center into a hard lower bound and could mislead a reader into thinking every 70 percent shooter must make at least 60 of every 100 attempts or that one unusual set proves the parameter changed.

expectedElements.description: Computes $z\approx-2.6$ and verifies $np=70$ and $n(1-p)=30$ are both at least 10
Calls 58 unusual while explaining that a low-probability binomial outcome still has positive probability
Explains that the coach treats the mean or typical range as a guaranteed cutoff and overclaims from one set

scoringGuide.E: Correctly computes and contextualizes the parameters and z-score, verifies both approximation counts, supports the analyst, and clearly explains both the rare-versus-zero distinction and the coach's misleading cutoff.
scoringGuide.P: Correctly identifies 58 as unusual with most calculations but omits an approximation count, the rare-versus-zero mechanism, or the specific consequence of the coach's statement.
scoringGuide.I: Uses 0.70 as the mean count, omits the square root in the standard deviation, calls 58 impossible, or treats the mean as a guaranteed result.

commonMistakes: Dividing 58 by the standard deviation instead of subtracting the mean first
Equating more than two standard deviations from the mean with zero probability

The coach confuses \blank[1.4in] with \blank[1.2in], which could make a reader believe \blank[2.3in].
